content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe different methods for measuring reaction rate
Choose appropriate methods for different reactions
Record and present rate data appropriately
To study how different factors affect reaction rate, we need reliable methods to measure it. The method chosen depends on the type of reaction and what changes can be observed.
The method depends on what changes during the reaction:
Time for colour to change, colorimeter
Time for solution to become opaque
Reactions that produce gas (gas escapes, mass decreases)
[DIAGRAM: Conical flask with marble chips and acid on a balance, cotton wool in top]
Place conical flask with acid on balance
Add marble chips and start timer
Loosely plug with cotton wool (prevents splashing but lets gas escape)
Small changes may be hard to detect
Doesn't work well for light gases (H₂)
[DIAGRAM: Conical flask connected via delivery tube to gas syringe]
Set up apparatus with reactants in flask
Add second reactant and start timer
Record volume of gas at regular intervals
Gases that don't dissolve much in water (H₂, O₂)
[DIAGRAM: Conical flask connected to inverted measuring cylinder filled with water in trough]
Fill measuring cylinder with water and invert in water trough
Connect flask to delivery tube under the cylinder
Record water displaced at regular intervals
[DIAGRAM: Conical flask on paper with cross, viewed from above]
Place flask on paper marked with a black cross
Stop timer when cross is no longer visible
Only gives one reading per experiment
Cannot plot rate vs time graph
Set up colorimeter with appropriate filter
Record at regular intervals (e.g., every 30 s)
Rate at a specific time (from graph):
Draw a tangent to the curve at that time
Calculate the gradient of the tangent
Suggest a suitable method to measure the rate of the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid.
This reaction produces hydrogen gas: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
to measure volume of hydrogen produced
(though H₂ is light so changes are small)
Best method: Gas syringe - accurate and continuous measurement.
From the data below, calculate the average rate between 0-60 seconds.
In a disappearing cross experiment, the cross disappeared after 45 seconds. In a repeat with higher concentration, it took 30 seconds. Which reaction was faster?
The reaction with higher concentration was faster
Rate ∝ 1/time, so rate increased from 1/45 to 1/30 = increased by factor of 1.5
Forgetting to start the timer immediately
Start timer as soon as reactants mix
Not sealing gas collection apparatus properly
Check for gas leaks before starting
Take frequent readings, especially at the start when rate is fastest
Describe how you would measure the rate of a reaction that produces carbon dioxide gas. (4 marks)

A student uses the disappearing cross method. Times recorded for three different concentrations were: 60 s, 40 s, and 25 s. a) Which concentration gave the fastest rate? (1 mark) b) Explain your answer. (2 marks)
Why is a gas syringe often preferred over measuring mass loss for gas-producing reactions? (2 marks)
Using the data in the table below, calculate: a) The average rate between 0 and 100 s (2 marks) b) The average rate between 100 and 200 s (2 marks) c) Explain why these rates are different. (2 marks)
Suggest why the disappearing cross method is less reliable than using a colorimeter. (2 marks)
Apparatus to measure volume of gas produced
Instrument that measures colour intensity of solutions
A straight line that touches a curve at one point
The slope of a line (change in y / change in x)
An insoluble solid formed during a reaction
Choose method based on what changes:
Gas produced → gas syringe, mass loss, collect over water
simple but less precise for light gases
simple, but subjective and gives single reading
Average rate = total change ÷ total time
gradient of tangent at a point
